turn_text: When you reflect back on your career, how did your parents influence your leadership style?

Well, your parents always influence who you are, what you are. And I was very fortunate to have a very to very solid people, people of good character as parents. They were children of the Depression. I know they were engaged to be married for about four or five years because they couldn't afford to get married. And then I was born in 1937, which was along toward the tail end of the Depression. But I think some of those values that people held as a result of that experience and depression years has stayed with me and that would be that you don't spend money if you don't have it. You try to make sure that what you spend your money on is worthwhile and that you can't count on prosperity and affluence lasting forever. And then beneath all of that was a very, very sound value system of honesty, integrity, a solid family that stuck together and through thick and thin had a difficult time because my dad was gone from 1941 to 1945. He was overseas in World War II in the European theater. I was in the Battle of the Bulge. My mom and I didn't hear from him for a period of about three months, and that was, of course, very nerve-wracking. And so they laid a good foundation. And when my dad came back, I didn't know him very well. I was five when he left, and I was about 10 when he came back. And one thing that I discovered was that he had a great love of athletics. and I wanted to please him and so I threw myself into athletics and so we had that in common and of course athletics has been a pretty dominant theme throughout my lifetime both as a player and then as a coach and now as an athletic director.

turn_text: Back to your book, we notice the foreword was written by one of your favorites of all time. John Wooden, tell us about your relationship with one of the greatest coaches to ever live.

Well, I first met John, who I don't know, it'd have been late 70s, early 80s. And he had gotten out of coaching, I think in 1976. And I think he was in Chicago to speak or something. And so I met him there and ran into him a couple other times and tucked him on the phone on occasion. And Nancy and I were able to go out and have lunch with him last January. And of course, he subsequently died about four months later. But John, the last time I saw him was 99, still very sharp. and probably of all the coaches that I've known, I admired him the most because he was very successful. He knew why he did things. He had a very strong philosophical base with a very spiritual person and I think had a great influence on those who played for him. So anyway, I've always admired him. He's written several books. I think I've read almost everything that he's written. And he had a great influence on me as a young coach because I read a book written by him. I think he might have been called, they call me coach or something like that. And in the book, he mentioned that he never talked about winning to his players. And I thought that was kind of unique because here was an individual who won more than anyone in basketball or football. And I think in a 12-year span, he won 10 national championships in basketball. And at one point, he had won 87, 88 straight games, home and away. And yet he never talked about winning. And he said that what he really emphasized was the process. And he quoted it as Cervantes. And Cervantes said something like this, the journey is more important than the end. What I took that to mean was that so often in coaching, we focus on wins and we focus on the final score, but the most important thing is really the journey, the relationships that are formed, the values that are taught, the daily grind, the work ethic, what you do in practice, how well you master the fundamentals. And so I took that as a great lesson and didn't talk to our players about winning. I never said, well, we have to win this game. And what we did, we talked about what we needed to do on Monday and Tuesday and Wednesday and talked about team chemistry and as time went on, of course, we We did win quite a few games, but it was always the focus was on the process.
